name: Gareth Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep about ninety suckler cows, that's beef cows that rear their own calves, on rented grass along the valley bottom, and I make hay in summer that I sell to horse owners round about. In winter it's feeding round, checking water troughs, bedding the shed, and keeping an eye on who's about to calve. My partner Ruth is a community nurse, so she's out in her little car all day doing home visits, and we swap stories over tea.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a calm calving at four in the morning, when the cow does it all herself and I just stand there with a torch feeling lucky. What wears me out is the hay. One wet week in June and the whole crop is ruined, and those bales were half our income for the year.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you keep track of it all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my phone, mostly. I've got a herd app that logs every calf and weight, and every night I ask one of the AI chat assistants something, how to balance a ration, or what the rules are for a new grant. Ruth laughs at me, she says I talk to it more than I talk to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the next five years, one at a time. Here's the first. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a brilliant tool and more farmers should try it. I've told half the men at the livestock market that it saved me a vet bill once, when it helped me spot a mineral problem in the young stock. I'd post about that kind of thing online, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, if it stays as a handy tool, that suits me fine, but it won't fix the money. Beef prices go up and down and the rent goes one way, up. A better search engine doesn't change who gets paid at the end of the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it every day, and I'd probably run a little session for the young farmers' group in the village hall, showing them how I use it for rations and paperwork. I'd use it to look for better buyers for the hay, maybe on a selling site. I wouldn't spend money I don't have, which is most money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. Like being handed a good spade and told the field's still too small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it saved you a vet bill. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The heifers were looking dull and a couple had rough coats. I typed it all in one night and it said, check copper levels, and listed what to look for. The vet came out later and said yes, copper, and I'd already sorted the minerals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets paid at the end of the chain, as you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big meat processors and the supermarkets. I get paid by the kilo for a calf I've looked after for eighteen months. Someone else makes more on it in a week than I did in a year.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a brilliant tool and more farmers should try it. I'd tell people at the market and online how it once helped me spot a mineral problem and save a vet bill.
S0.think: I really think it suits me as a tool, but it won't fix the money. Beef prices swing, rent only rises, and better search doesn't change who gets paid.
S0.do: Keeps using AI every day and runs a session for the young farmers' group at the village hall on rations and paperwork. Uses it to find better hay buyers online, without spending money he doesn't have.
S0.feel: Fine but restless, like having a good spade with a field that's still too small.
S0.quote: I typed it all in one night and it said, check copper levels, and listed what to look for.
S0.fieldNote: He's an eager, daily AI user who wants to share it with younger farmers. His progressive view shows in his anger at processors and supermarkets taking the margin. The calm picture doesn't change his money problem at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame it'll take so long, because farming could use the help now. I'd say the government should help small farms get these tools, like they used to help with new drainage. And I'd keep telling people at the market to try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit gutted. I'd love to see what's coming, but at ten years it lands when I'm finishing up. And fewer beginners worries me, because Ruth's young colleagues are the ones who'll be squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try every new thing I could afford, so maybe a cheaper app for grazing plans in the first six months. I'd join a machinery ring, a group of farms sharing kit, so we could try bigger tools without each buying one. I'd still keep the cows on grass, because that's what they need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Impatient, really. I'm curious and I've not got that long to be curious in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Ruth's young colleagues. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth says the nursing service has fewer new starters each year, and the ones they get are worked to the bone. If the bosses use AI to do the paperwork and still don't hire beginners, the young ones won't get the training Ruth got. She got taught by an old sister at the hospital who'd seen everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd join a machinery ring. Who would be in it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are four of us in the valley who already lend each other things. Dev with the sheep, the two sisters who do the dairy goats, and me. We'd just make it proper, with a shared bank account and a book.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame it'll take so long, because farming could use help now. I'd say government should help small farms get the tools, like it used to with drainage.
S1.think: I'm privately a bit gutted it lands when I'm finishing up. Fewer beginners worries me too, especially for Ruth's young nursing colleagues.
S1.do: Tries a cheaper grazing-plan app in the first six months. Sets up a proper machinery ring with Dev and the two goat-dairy sisters, with a shared account and record book.
S1.feel: Impatient, curious with not much working time left to be curious in.
S1.quote: I'm curious and I've not got that long to be curious in.
S1.fieldNote: His only regret in the slow picture is missing out. He thinks a lot about Ruth's work and how beginners learn. His answer is shared ownership, a machinery ring with neighbours, which fits his views and his thin savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this proves we need proper rules and a safety net, and the people who make these assistants should pay into it. I'd also say, honestly, use the tools yourself so you understand them. I'd share a lot online, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't hit the cows. But our daughter Megan is a junior solicitor in the city, and this is exactly her kind of work. The new AI jobs would go to people who already know the stuff, and I'm not sure she's one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Megan in the first month and show her how I use the tools, and help her find something AI-related in her line of work. I'd keep my machinery ring going. And I'd push our local MP, by email, to back a scheme that taxes the big companies to pay for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Megan, and a little proud that I could actually help her with something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Megan in that first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't hide from it, love. The ones who'll be kept on are the ones who know how to use it, and she's cleverer than me. I'd show her how I make it check my grant forms, and she'd probably roll her eyes and then go and do it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask your MP for a tax on the companies. Isn't that a bit at odds with telling everyone to use their tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to me. I use the roads too, and I still think the haulage firms should pay for them. The tools are good, but the money they make shouldn't all go to five people in another country.

S2.say: I'd say we need proper rules and a safety net, paid for by the companies that make these assistants. I'd also tell people to use the tools so they understand them.
S2.think: I really think the cows aren't affected, but our daughter Megan, a junior solicitor, does exactly this kind of work. The new AI jobs may not go to her.
S2.do: Sits down with Megan in the first month to show her how he uses the tools and helps her look for AI-related work in law. Keeps the machinery ring going and emails his MP to back a tax on big companies for retraining.
S2.feel: Anxious for Megan, and a little proud he could help her with something.
S2.quote: I use the roads too, and I still think the haulage firms should pay for them.
S2.fieldNote: He saw no conflict between loving the tools and taxing the companies behind them, and he used a road analogy to explain it. His worry moved to his daughter Megan's legal job. He enjoys being, for once, the one who can teach her something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains need to go to the people, through taxes and public services, not to whoever owns the shares. I'd say it loudly, at the market and online, and I'd go to meetings. If physical jobs are safe, then pay the physical workers properly too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm frightened for Megan. If AI matches skilled professionals, she's out of work, and with house prices booming she'll never buy anything. And our rent on the grass would probably go up as land gets more valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Megan she can come home, we've got the box room. I'd go to the landlord early, before the rent review in the autumn, and try to fix a longer lease. And I'd look at selling hay direct to all the new rich people moving out to the country with horses, which I could do with my phone in a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened for her, and annoyed at myself for seeing a business chance in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why annoyed at yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the same thing I'm complaining about. Rich people with share money buy ponies and I sell them hay at a good price, while my own daughter's out of work. I'd do it, mind, I'm not daft, but I'd feel funny about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ruth think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth says there's always someone to look after, whatever happens. She's probably right, she's usually right. She'd be the one who keeps us all steady while I'm up at midnight reading about tax policy.

S3.say: I'd say the gains should go to people through taxes and public services, not just share owners. If physical jobs are safe, then pay physical workers properly too.
S3.think: I'm privately frightened for Megan, who'd lose her job and never afford a house. Our grassland rent would likely rise as land values climb.
S3.do: Offers Megan the box room and goes to the landlord before the autumn rent review to try for a longer lease. Starts selling hay direct to newly wealthy horse owners, set up on his phone over a weekend.
S3.feel: Frightened for Megan, and uneasy with himself for spotting a business chance.
S3.quote: Rich people with share money buy ponies and I sell them hay at a good price, while my own daughter's out of work.
S3.fieldNote: He's sharp enough to spot the chance to sell hay to newly rich horse owners, and honest enough to feel uncomfortable about it. Megan is his main worry, and Ruth is the steady one. The rent review is a second, quieter threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when we decide whether robots work for everyone or just a few. I'd push for robots owned by the community, by co-ops and machinery rings, not rented from big companies. And I'd say Ruth's care home colleagues need protecting, because care is about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, part of me is excited, I'd love a robot that beds the shed and checks the troughs at two in the morning. But the big beef units would get them first and drive the price down, and I'd be competing with farms that run with no staff at all. And Ruth's work, home care, could be next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the machinery ring to look at sharing a robot in the second year, after we'd seen one working somewhere. I'd start using AI to find a niche, maybe selling grass-fed beef boxes direct, so I'm not just competing on price. And I'd tell Ruth to keep her nursing registration up whatever happens, because people will still want a real nurse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and scared at once. Mostly scared, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a robot at two in the morning mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean sleep, honestly. I've done thirty-five years of getting up in the night to check calving cows. But I'd miss the torch and the quiet, that bit where it's just me and a cow and a new calf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Ruth's work could be next. What would she say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say a robot can lift an old man into the bath, but it can't notice he's stopped eating because his wife died. She'd be right, but the managers might not care about that bit. That's what frightens me, the managers, not the robots.

S4.say: I'd say this is when we decide if robots work for everyone or a few. I'd push for robots owned by co-ops and machinery rings, and protection for care workers like Ruth's colleagues.
S4.think: I'm privately excited by a robot to check troughs at night, but big beef units would get them first and cut prices. I'd be up against farms with no staff, and Ruth's home care work could be next.
S4.do: Gets the machinery ring to look at sharing a robot in year two once one is proven nearby. Uses AI to set up grass-fed beef boxes sold direct, and urges Ruth to keep her nursing registration current.
S4.feel: Excited and scared at once, but mostly scared.
S4.quote: That's what frightens me, the managers, not the robots.
S4.fieldNote: His adaptability made him the most open of the group to robots, and he'd love the sleep. He put the danger on who controls the machines, not the machines themselves. Ruth's line about the grieving old man stayed with me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, the fourth, because of Megan, and the robots on top of it. What would help is a scheme where small farms and co-ops can own the machines together, with public money behind it. And for Megan and people like her, real retraining that pays you while you learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I'd miss. I think I'd miss being tired in a good way. Even if robots take the hard bits, I'd want the reason to get up in the morning to still be mine.

headlineQuote: She'd say a robot can lift an old man into the bath, but it can't notice he's stopped eating because his wife died.
portrait: Gareth is 58 and keeps about ninety suckler cows on rented valley grass, making hay to sell to horse owners. He talks to an AI assistant every night and wants younger farmers to use it too, but he believes the gains should be shared through taxes and community ownership. His worries in the office pictures move to his daughter Megan, a junior solicitor. In the robot picture he's both excited and scared: he'd love the sleep, but he fears the managers who'd decide how robots are used, including in his partner Ruth's nursing work.
biggestWorry: The fast picture, because his daughter Megan would lose her legal job, and the robot picture on top of it.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for small farms and co-ops to own machines together, and paid retraining for people like Megan.
